usage: polite present; 하다-adjective, so 하 + 여요 contracts to 해요 — the most common spoken form
to feel a weight off one's chest
set phrase; literally 'the insides feel clear' — say this after venting or finishing something
adverb form (하다→하게), e.g. 후련하게 울다 to have a good cleansing cry
-아/어지다 attaches to the 해 stem and shows the shift from heavy to light
examples: 시험 끝나서 후련해요.
I'm relieved the exam is over.
simple 해요 form; use it when a stressful thing is done, not just when you're happy
할 말을 다 하고 나니까 속이 후련하네요.
Now that I've said everything I wanted to, I feel so relieved.
-고 나니까 'now that I've finished ~' frames the classic after-venting context
몇 년 묵은 고민을 털어놓고 나니까 가슴이 다 후련하더라고요.
After finally pouring out a worry I'd carried for years, my chest felt completely clear.
real-situation; 다 here is intensifier 'completely', and -더라고요 reports the felt experience
nuance: 후련하다 names the clean, lightened sensation right after a burden or pent-up stress is released — finishing exams, finally venting, crying it out. Its near-synonym is 시원하다: 시원하다 is the broader word that also covers physical coolness (시원한 바람, a cool breeze) and refreshing drinks, while 후련하다 is reserved almost entirely for emotional/internal release, so '속이 후련하다' and '속이 시원하다' overlap but 바람이 후련하다 is wrong. It is NOT general happiness (기쁘다/행복하다) — it strictly presupposes something heavy was weighing on you and is now gone. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 후련해요 / 후련했어요 / 후련해서, and it collocates above all with 속이, 가슴이, and the adverb 후련하게. English-speaker pitfall: learners reach for it as a synonym of 'happy', but if there was no preceding pressure to discharge, a Korean ear hears it as odd — 'I'm 후련해' out of plain good cheer sounds like a non sequitur.

Saying '후련 있어요' (treating it like a noun) is wrong; it is an adjective, so conjugate it directly: 후련해요, 후련했어요.

english: uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling
usage: polite present; 하다-adjective contracting to 해요 — common after an awkward or unresolved moment
뭔가 ('somehow/something') is the habitual partner adverb that triggers this word
adverb form, e.g. 찝찝하게 헤어졌어요 we parted on an unsettled note
examples: 뭔가 찝찝해요.
Something just feels off.
the bare, high-frequency form; 뭔가 sets up the vague unease
사과는 받았는데 뭔가 찝찝하네요.
I got an apology, but something still feels off.
-는데 contrasts the apology with the lingering residue; use when a resolution doesn't fully satisfy
계약서에 도장 찍긴 했는데 조건이 영 찝찝해서 다시 읽어 봤어요.
I did stamp the contract, but the terms left me so uneasy that I reread it.
real-situation; 영 'utterly' + 찝찝해서 'because it felt off' gives the cause that drove an action
nuance: 찝찝하다 is the nagging, not-quite-resolved discomfort that sticks to you — a conversation that ended badly, a decision you can't fully trust, even a slightly unclean feeling on your skin. Contrast it sharply with 불안하다: 불안하다 is forward-looking anxiety about what might happen, whereas 찝찝하다 is the backward-looking residue of something that already occurred and didn't settle cleanly. It is milder than 죄책감 (guilt) — more 'this won't sit right' than 'I did wrong'. It lives in casual speech and pairs constantly with 뭔가, 영, and 기분/느낌. Note the spelling: the standard dictionary form is 찜찜하다, but 찝찝하다 is the more emphatic, far more common everyday variant. English-speaker pitfall: learners map it to 'uncomfortable' and then misuse it for physical pain (a sore back is 아프다/불편하다, not 찝찝하다); 찝찝하다 is psychological/residual unease, or at most a faint 'icky, not-clean' feeling.

Using it in formal writing or a business report reads as too casual/slangy; in those registers prefer 꺼림칙하다 or 마음에 걸리다.

english: overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle
usage: polite present; stem 벅차- already ends in ㅏ so it just adds 요 — context decides positive vs negative
set phrase; with 가슴이 it is the moved/overcome-by-joy sense
attributive form (차다→찬); common with 감동, 행복, 순간
adverb form, e.g. 벅차게 다가오다 to hit one overwhelmingly
examples: 일이 좀 벅차요.
The work is a bit too much for me.
simple form, practical sense: a load exceeds your capacity
첫 월급을 받으니까 가슴이 벅차네요.
Getting my first paycheck, my heart just swells.
the positive 'overcome with emotion' sense; 가슴이 is the tell
혼자 부모님 병간호까지 하려니 솔직히 벅차서 동생한테 도움을 청했어요.
Caring for my parents alone on top of everything was honestly too much, so I asked my younger sibling for help.
real-situation; -려니 'when I try to' + 벅차서 gives the reason for an action
nuance: 벅차다 carries two flavors that share one root idea — 'more than the vessel can hold'. One is the heart-swelling kind: overcome with joy, pride, or gratitude (가슴이 벅차다). The other is the practical kind: a workload or responsibility that exceeds your capacity (일이 벅차다). The 가슴이 + 벅차다 frame is almost always the warm, positive reading; a task as subject flips it to the stressful 'I can't cope' reading. Contrast it with 바쁘다: 바쁘다 only means you have a lot to do (busy), while 벅차다 says the amount is beyond what you can manage — you could be 안 바쁘다 yet still find one hard task 벅차다. Note 벅차다 is its own adjective, not a 하다-word, so the stem is 벅차- (벅차요, 벅찼어요, 벅차서, 벅찬). English-speaker pitfall: assuming it is always positive because of its frequent use in emotional moments — '일이 벅차다' is a genuine cry that something is too much.

english: empty; feeling a void; missing something
usage: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, for emotional emptiness
to feel a void in one's heart
set phrase for loneliness or loss; 마음이 is the default subject
adverb form, e.g. 집이 허전하게 느껴져요 the house feels empty
examples: 혼자 있으니까 좀 허전해요.
Being alone, I feel a bit empty.
simple form; the basic 'a void is here' use
룸메이트가 이사 가니까 집이 너무 허전해요.
Now that my roommate moved out, the place feels so empty.
the void left when someone is gone; subject can be a place, not just a person's heart
20년 키운 강아지를 떠나보내고 나니 집안 곳곳이 허전해서 한동안 적응이 안 됐어요.
After saying goodbye to the dog I'd raised for 20 years, every corner of the house felt so empty that I couldn't adjust for a while.
real-situation; 곳곳이 'in every corner' + 허전해서 conveys pervasive absence
nuance: 허전하다 is the quiet, wistful emptiness left behind when something or someone familiar is missing — a friend moves away, a long routine ends, a pet passes, or you just feel a vague hollow. Contrast it with 외롭다: 외롭다 specifically means lonely/alone (a person without company), whereas 허전하다 is about a felt absence or void that can apply even in a crowd when something expected is gone — you can be surrounded by people and still 허전하다 because a particular presence is missing. It is gentler than 슬프다 (active sorrow); 허전하다 is hollowness, not crying. Notably it attaches not only to 마음/가슴 but to places (집이 허전하다) and even body parts (목이 허전하다 after a haircut, 손이 허전하다 without a ring). English-speaker pitfall: translating 'I miss you' as '당신이 허전해요' — that is wrong; 허전하다 describes the void you feel, not the act of missing a person. For 'I miss you' use 보고 싶어요.

usage: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a very common compliment-adjacent word
set phrase; you feel backed-up and safe, 마음이 as subject
attributive form (하다→한); high praise for a friend or colleague
adverb form, e.g. 든든하게 먹다 to eat a hearty, filling meal
examples: 네가 있어서 든든해.
Having you here, I feel reassured.
casual 반말; warm thing to say to a close friend
아침 든든하게 먹고 나왔어요.
I had a hearty breakfast before heading out.
the 'pleasantly full and fueled' sense; 든든하게 + 먹다 collocation
보험까지 들어 두니 무슨 일이 생겨도 마음이 든든해서 발 뻗고 자게 돼요.
Now that I've even taken out insurance, I feel so secure that I can sleep soundly whatever happens.
real-situation; the safety-net sense, with 발 뻗고 자다 'sleep with legs stretched = at ease'
nuance: 든든하다 is the warm feeling of being backed up and secure — a dependable person at your side, a financial safety net, or a filling meal that fuels you for the day. Contrast it with 안심하다: 안심하다 is a verb meaning 'to feel relieved / set one's mind at ease' about a specific worry that has resolved, while 든든하다 is the standing, ongoing sense of having reliable support behind you (a backbone, not a resolved worry). Calling a person 든든하다 (그 사람 참 든든해요) is genuine praise for reliability. With food it means satisfyingly full and energized — more than 배부르다 (merely full): 든든하다 adds 'well-prepared, set up to go'. As a 하다-adjective it gives 든든해요 / 든든했어요 / 든든해서, and collocates with 마음이, 사람, and 든든하게 먹다. English-speaker pitfall: saying '저는 든든해요' to mean 'I am a reliable person' — Korean uses it for the reassurance you feel from something/someone, so frame it as 마음이 든든해요 or 그 사람이 든든해요.

Saying '저는 든든한 사람이에요' to boast that you yourself are dependable sounds odd; let others call you 든든하다. Describe the feeling you give: '제가 있으면 든든하시죠?' is more natural, or just say 믿음직하다 of yourself sparingly.
Treating it as identical to 안심하다 is imprecise: 안심하다 (verb) = a worry resolved; 든든하다 (adjective) = ongoing backing/support behind you.

english: light and unburdened; free of a load
usage: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, said when a responsibility ends
adverb form, e.g. 홀가분하게 떠나다 to leave unburdened
examples: 일 끝나서 홀가분해요.
Work's done, so I feel light and free.
simple form; the relief of shedding a task
짐 다 부치고 홀가분하게 여행 다녔어요.
I shipped all my luggage and traveled light and carefree.
literal lightness blending into emotional lightness; 홀가분하게 + 다니다
오래 끌던 소송이 끝나니 어깨에 얹혔던 짐을 내려놓은 듯 홀가분하더라고요.
When the long-dragging lawsuit ended, I felt as unburdened as if I'd set down a load on my shoulders.
real-situation; the 듯 simile spells out the 'weight set down for good' core meaning
nuance: 홀가분하다 is the buoyant lightness you feel after putting down a long-carried load — finishing a major project, paying off debt, ending an obligation. Contrast it carefully with its closest neighbor 후련하다: 후련하다 emphasizes the cathartic discharge of pent-up stress (the release), whereas 홀가분하다 emphasizes the resulting freedom and mobility (the lightness that remains) — after finally telling someone off you are 후련하다 (it came out), but after a years-long duty finally ends you are 홀가분하다 (you're free now). It implies a relatively lasting relief, not a fleeting one, and pairs above all with 마음이, 어깨, and 홀가분하게 떠나다/다니다. As a 하다-adjective: 홀가분해요 / 홀가분했어요 / 홀가분해서. English-speaker pitfall: using it for a momentary 'phew' — 홀가분하다 should mark a real burden that has been set down for good, so for a quick instant of relief 후련하다 or 다행이다 fits better.

usage: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, describes the relationship's distance
reduplicated form that intensifies and softens the awkwardness, very common in speech
attributive form (하다→한); 사이 = the relationship between people
adverb form, e.g. 서먹하게 인사하다 to greet stiffly
examples: 우리 아직 좀 서먹해요.
We're still a little distant with each other.
simple form; states the relationship is not yet close
같은 팀이지만 아직 서먹해요.
We're on the same team, but it's still awkward between us.
-지만 contrast frames not-yet-close coworkers
10년 만에 만난 동창들과 처음엔 서먹했는데 술 한잔하니 금세 옛날로 돌아갔어요.
With classmates I met after 10 years it was awkward at first, but after a drink we quickly went back to the old days.
real-situation; shows 서먹하다 as the dissolvable distance of a long gap
nuance: 서먹하다 describes the awkward, not-yet-comfortable distance BETWEEN people who aren't close — new coworkers, friends after a long gap, two people after a quarrel. It is fundamentally relational. Contrast it with 어색하다 and 멋쩍다, the words learners confuse it with: 어색하다 covers awkwardness in general including situations and one's own self-consciousness (어색한 분위기, an awkward vibe; 어색한 미소, a forced smile), and 멋쩍다 is purely your own sheepish embarrassment — but 서먹하다 specifically names the coolness of a relationship, the gap of unfamiliarity between two parties. The reduplicated 서먹서먹하다 is idiomatic and a touch more vivid. As a 하다-adjective: 서먹해요 / 서먹했어요 / 서먹해서, and it pairs with 사이, 둘이, 분위기. English-speaker pitfall: using 서먹하다 for your own embarrassment ('칭찬받아서 서먹했어요') is wrong — that personal sheepishness is 멋쩍다/어색하다; 서먹하다 needs two parties and a relationship.

Saying you are 서먹하다 by yourself ('저 혼자 서먹해요') is wrong; it always needs a relationship — frame it as 둘이 서먹하다 or 사이가 서먹하다.
Confusing it with 낯설다 ('이 동네가 서먹해요') is wrong; for an unfamiliar place/thing use 낯설다, reserve 서먹하다 for the coolness between people.

english: displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving
usage: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, expresses disapproval of something
attributive form (하다→한); very common with 표정/얼굴/눈빛
adverb form, e.g. 못마땅하게 쳐다보다 to glare disapprovingly
examples: 나는 그 결정이 못마땅해.
I'm not happy with that decision.
casual 반말; the basic 'it doesn't sit right with me' use
엄마는 내 결정이 못마땅한 표정이셨어요.
Mom had a disapproving look about my decision.
the classic 못마땅한 표정 collocation; note the senior-reacts-to-junior pattern
부장님은 신입의 복장이 영 못마땅하신지 회의 내내 인상을 쓰고 계셨어요.
The manager, apparently quite displeased with the new hire's outfit, kept frowning throughout the meeting.
real-situation; 못마땅하신지 'seemingly displeased' + honorific 시 shows third-person disapproval shown by face
nuance: 못마땅하다 means something does not sit right with you — you disapprove of or find it unsatisfactory. The word transparently builds from 마땅하다 ('to be proper/fitting') negated by 못, so it literally reads 'not as it ought to be', which is exactly its flavor: a falling-short of your standard. It is typically shown through the face (못마땅한 표정/눈빛) rather than declared, and very often features a senior reacting to a junior's choice. Contrast it with 화나다: 화나다 is active anger that flares, whereas 못마땅하다 is quiet, simmering disapproval/dissatisfaction — you can be 못마땅하다 for days without ever being 화나다. Crucially, because it is an adjective of feeling, describing a THIRD person's displeasure requires 못마땅해하다 (부장님이 못마땅해하셨어요), not bare 못마땅하다. English-speaker pitfall: saying '엄마가 못마땅해요' to mean 'Mom is displeased' — that wrongly says 'I am displeased with Mom'; switch to 엄마가 못마땅해하세요.

usage: I'm displeased / I'm in a bad mood
polite present; the ㅎ of the ㄶ batchim is silent, so it's pronounced [언짜나요]
to be in a sour mood
set phrase; 기분이 is the usual subject
attributive form (ㄶ stem + 은 → 언짢은); 기색 = a visible sign of a feeling
adverb form, e.g. 언짢게 듣다 to take something the wrong way
examples: 그 말 때문에 좀 언짢았어요.
That remark put me in a bit of a sour mood.
simple past; reacting to something mildly offensive
혹시 제 말 때문에 기분 언짢으셨다면 죄송해요.
If what I said happened to put you in a bad mood, I'm sorry.
the very common polite apology frame 기분 언짢으셨다면
사장님이 아침부터 무슨 일이 있으셨는지 종일 언짢은 기색이라 다들 눈치만 봤어요.
The boss had a displeased air all day as if something had happened in the morning, so everyone just read the room.
real-situation; 언짢은 기색 + 눈치 보다 paints reading a superior's sour mood
nuance: 언짢다 describes being in a displeased, slightly offended, sour mood — how you feel when something rubs you the wrong way but you're not full-blown angry. Contrast it with two neighbors: 못마땅하다 points outward at a specific thing you disapprove of (a choice, conduct), while 언짢다 points inward at your own soured emotional state/mood; and 화나다 is hot, flaring anger, whereas 언짢다 is a cooler, lower-grade displeasure. It appears constantly in courteous apologies — '기분 언짢으셨다면 죄송합니다' is a fixed politeness formula. Watch the pronunciation: the ㄶ batchim keeps its spelling but the ㅎ is not separately pronounced, so 언짢아요 sounds like [언짜나요] and 언짢다 like [언짠타]. English-speaker pitfall: respelling it phonetically as 언잖다 or 언짠다 because the ㅎ is inaudible — the correct spelling is always 언짢다 with ㄶ.

usage: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a gentle, satisfied warmth
attributive form (하다→한); very common with 미소/표정
set phrase; the prototypical action that goes with this feeling
adverb form modifying verbs like 보다, 웃다
examples: 그 소식을 들으니 흐뭇해요.
Hearing that news, I feel warm and pleased.
simple form; quiet pleasure at a good outcome
아이들 노는 거 보니까 흐뭇하네요.
Watching the kids play, I feel so warm inside.
the classic context: contentment watching others do well
손주가 의젓하게 인사하는 모습을 할머니가 흐뭇한 미소로 바라보셨어요.
Grandmother watched with a contented smile as her grandchild greeted everyone so maturely.
real-situation; 흐뭇한 미소 + 바라보다, the signature 'wear it on your face' pairing
nuance: 흐뭇하다 is a warm, gentle contentment — the soft, slightly proud satisfaction of seeing something turn out well, especially OTHERS doing well (kids at play, a junior succeeding, a grandchild behaving). Contrast it with 뿌듯하다 and 자랑스럽다, the words learners blur it with: 뿌듯하다 is the chest-filling pride you feel about your OWN achievement or close stake (시험에 붙어서 뿌듯해요), and 자랑스럽다 is 'proud (of)' often said outward; but 흐뭇하다 is the mellow, observing warmth of an onlooker pleased by a heartwarming scene, calmer and more tender than excited pride. Because it is often worn on the face, it pairs idiomatically with 미소, 표정, and 바라보다. As a 하다-adjective: 흐뭇해요 / 흐뭇했어요 / 흐뭇해서; for a third person's contentment use 흐뭇해하다 (부모님이 흐뭇해하셨어요). English-speaker pitfall: reaching for it about your own big win — '시험 붙어서 흐뭇해요' sounds detached; for personal achievement say 뿌듯하다.

english: deeply moved; choked up with emotion
usage: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a sudden welling of emotion
set phrase; the most common frame, 가슴이 as subject
to get choked up (the nose tingles)
vivid set phrase for that nearly-tearing-up moment
adverb form, e.g. 뭉클하게 다가오다 to hit one emotionally
examples: 그 장면이 뭉클했어요.
That scene was moving.
simple past; the basic 'it touched me' use
부모님 편지를 읽고 가슴이 뭉클했어요.
Reading my parents' letter, I got all choked up.
the prototypical heartfelt context; 가슴이 뭉클하다
참전 용사들이 서로 끌어안는 장면에서 나도 모르게 코끝이 뭉클해지더라고요.
At the scene where the war veterans embraced, my nose tingled with tears before I knew it.
real-situation; 코끝이 뭉클해지다 + 나도 모르게 'without realizing' captures the involuntary surge
nuance: 뭉클하다 is the sudden lump-in-the-throat, heart-swelling rush of being deeply moved — a heartfelt letter, a reunion, a touching scene. The word is mimetic: 뭉클 evokes a soft mass welling up and pressing, so it captures the PHYSICAL sensation of emotion rising. Contrast it with 감동하다 (a verb, 'to be touched/impressed'): 감동하다 is the broader, more general statement that you were moved or impressed (even intellectually), whereas 뭉클하다 zeroes in on the warm, almost-teary bodily welling-up in a single instant — you can be 감동했어요 by an admirable feat without being 뭉클; 뭉클 needs the throat-tightening tenderness. It pairs idiomatically with 가슴이 and the very evocative 코끝이. As a 하다-adjective: 뭉클해요 / 뭉클했어요 / 뭉클해서. English-speaker pitfall: using it for cool intellectual admiration ('그 논문이 뭉클해요') is wrong — that is 인상적이다/감동적이다; 뭉클하다 is the momentary emotional, near-teary reaction, not 'impressive'.

usage: polite present; stem 멋쩍- + 어요 (ㄱ batchim), for mild self-conscious embarrassment
attributive form (멋쩍- + 은); the signature collocation
set phrase for the awkward laugh you give when embarrassed
-아/어하다 form to describe someone else looking sheepish
examples: 칭찬받으니까 좀 멋쩍어요.
Getting praised makes me feel a bit sheepish.
simple form; the classic trigger — praise you don't know how to take
할 말이 없어서 멋쩍게 웃었어요.
I had nothing to say, so I just laughed sheepishly.
the awkward-laugh reflex; 멋쩍게 웃다 is the go-to collocation
사람들 앞에서 발표하다 이름을 까먹어서 머리만 긁으며 멋쩍게 서 있었어요.
I forgot the name mid-presentation in front of everyone and just stood there sheepishly scratching my head.
real-situation; mild public embarrassment plus the head-scratch gesture, not deep shame
nuance: 멋쩍다 is that mild, sheepish self-consciousness — being complimented, caught in a small slip, or left with nothing to say, so you give an awkward little laugh. Contrast it with 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: 부끄럽다 covers shyness or genuine shame, and 창피하다 is stronger 'embarrassing/mortifying' (a real loss of face), whereas 멋쩍다 is the lightest of the three — a momentary, almost endearing social awkwardness with no real shame, the feeling behind a bashful grin. Note it is NOT a 하다-adjective: the stem is 멋쩍- (멋쩍어요, 멋쩍었어요, 멋쩍어서, 멋쩍은), and the ㄱ batchim takes 어 not 해. It collocates above all with 웃음 and 웃다 (멋쩍은 웃음, 멋쩍게 웃다). English-speaker pitfall: confusing it with 서먹하다 — 멋쩍다 is your OWN in-the-moment sheepishness, while 서먹하다 is the distance BETWEEN two people, so they are not swappable.
